sentences.text: Byronosaurus was a small troodontid dinosaur that lived in Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous Period.
This animal measured between 1.5 and 2 meters in length, stood 50 centimeters tall, and weighed between 4 and 20 kilograms.
Unlike most of its relatives, Byronosaurus lacked serrations on its teeth, a primitive trait also seen in the relative Xixiasaurus.
Researchers suggested that juvenile skulls found in an oviraptorid nest were washed there from a nearby Byronosaurus nest by water flow.
Michael Novacek discovered the first skeleton of Byronosaurus in 1993 at Ukhaa Tolgod in the Gobi Desert.
A second specimen, a skull, was discovered on July 15, 1996, at the Bolor's Hill site approximately eight kilometers from the original find.
Troodontids, including Byronosaurus, possessed some of the highest encephalization quotients among non-avian dinosaurs.
Large eye-sockets and well-developed middle-ears suggest that troodontids like Byronosaurus had keen senses.
Proportionately long legs indicate that troodontids like Byronosaurus were agile.
In 2001, Philip J. Currie and Dong Zhiming argued that troodontids were carnivorous, noting their anatomy and serrated teeth were consistent with a meat-eating lifestyle.
Researchers suggested that the loss of serrations in Byronosaurus teeth indicates a dietary shift, possibly making these animals herbivorous or omnivorous.
In 2017, researchers suggested that juvenile specimens previously assigned to Byronosaurus actually belong to Almas ukhae due to differences in skull features like the number of maxillary teeth.
Some researchers dispute the assignment of the juvenile skulls to Byronosaurus, citing skull morphology differences and suggesting they may not belong to the genus.
